clue.text: One beginning to position essential pockets inside setter's coat? Good Lord!

indicators.note: inside says the following group of letters sits within the coat

parts.note: a setter is a gundog, and its coat is its hairs
one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: pockets means the word for essential holds the next letter like a pocket

parts.note: something essential is a must

indicators.note: beginning to asks for only the opening letter of position

explanation.surface: A setter asks someone to tuck an important item into his coat, then exclaims in exasperation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setter' is not Paul but a gundog, whose coat is hair; the phrase is a facetious name for God, so 'Good Lord!' doubles as an exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: A jocular phrase for God, the deity thought of as living above us, and so a fair stand-in for the Lord.

clue.text: While bottle after spinning stopped by hapless Beth, play dirty

indicators.note: stopped by means the first jumble is plugged by the second, which sits inside it
after spinning says the letters of the first two words have been whirled into a new order
hapless means unfortunate and in a mess, so the name's letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Spin the bottle goes wrong when unlucky Beth halts it and someone cheats at the game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'While' is not a conjunction but fodder: 'after spinning' jumbles WHILE BOTTLE, 'hapless' jumbles the name, and 'stopped by' plugs the second jumble into the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom from boxing, where a punch below the waistband is illegal, so it means act unfairly.

clue.text: What covers Paul's bald patch well!

definitions.meaning: Paul is the setter, so his headgear is the setter's own cap, said in the first person
an exclamation of surprise, like 'goodness me!'

explanation.surface: The setter jokes about his own baldness and what hides it.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an old exclamation of surprise, and literally the setter speaking of the cap on his own head.

clue.text: Opening time — charge!

parts.note: a job opening is a vacant post
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Like a call to arms: the doors open and the crowd is told to rush in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charge!' looks like a battle cry; it is the fee for sending a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The fee paid to send mail is the cost, or charge, of delivery.

clue.text: Great Hollywood success

definitions.meaning: the 1997 James Cameron film about the sunken liner, a huge box-office hit

explanation.surface: A film earns praise as a big Hollywood hit.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means gigantic, and the same word names the record-breaking 1997 blockbuster.

clue.text: Quaffing vat, what giant might say, drinking

indicators.note: quaffing means swallowing, so the giant's words take the container inside them

parts.note: a giant might boast 'I'm big'
a bin is a large storage container, like a vat

explanation.surface: A giant gulps down a whole vat while boasting about his size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quaffing' looks like the definition, but it is the container signal; 'drinking' at the end defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Swallowing liquid, especially alcohol, is the sense shared by the two participles.

clue.text: Is it complete? Show part of it in full

definitions.text: Is it complete? Show part of it in full

parts.words: Is it complete? Show part of it in full
parts.note: the short form SITCOM lurks within 'Is it complete', and 'in full' asks for it spelt out at length; 'Show' says what kind of thing it is

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a job is finished and asks to see a section of it fully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part of it' points to SITCOM, held within 'iS IT COMplete'; 'in full' expands that abbreviation into its two full words, a type of Show.
explanation.definitionFit: A television comedy built on recurring characters in comic situations, the long form of the abbreviation sitcom.

clue.text: What might have come before G Plan, briefly — something cast in gutter?

parts.words: What might have come before G
parts.note: F precedes G in the alphabet

indicators.note: briefly means the word for plan is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: an agenda is a plan of business

explanation.surface: Musing on what preceded G Plan furniture, then spotting rubbish thrown in the gutter.
explanation.walkthrough: G Plan is a British furniture brand; the clue splits it as G, which F precedes, and 'Plan', which gives AGEND(A) by 'briefly'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cigarette butt, slang for the stub that smokers flick into the gutter.

clue.text: How one might learn some of the Tory backbenchers turned up

indicators.note: in a down entry, turned up means the letters read from bottom to top
some of means only a run of letters inside the phrase is taken

explanation.surface: Tory MPs at the back of the Commons have rebelled or shown up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some of' takes ETORYB from 'thE TORY Backbenchers'; 'turned up' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: Learning by mechanical repetition and memory, without understanding, is a way of studying.

clue.text: See 13
See 17
Problem looking OK with school after low grade

indicators.note: after says the next two parts follow the grade letter

parts.note: E is a low exam grade
OK means yes
to school is to train or teach

explanation.surface: A pupil's problem seems fine once they have schooling after a poor mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Problem looking' reads as 'problem seeming'; it is a problem with looking.
explanation.definitionFit: Tired, aching eyes are a trouble with seeing, so this is a difficulty in looking.

clue.text: A royal disapproval for party?

parts.note: Bea is Princess Beatrice, a member of the British royal family
saying no expresses disapproval

explanation.surface: Asks whether a monarch's frown is the reason for some event.
explanation.walkthrough: BEA is Princess Beatrice, granddaughter of Elizabeth II.
explanation.definitionFit: A British informal word for a lively celebration or knees-up.

clue.text: Processing Spoonerised chat, make not a lot of habit etc?

definitions.text: make not a lot of habit etc?

indicators.note: processing means working material over into a new form, so these letters are reworked

explanation.surface: Talk mangled by swapped sounds somehow shrinks a habit into something small.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoonerised' looks like a Spoonerism signal; it is only fodder. Leaving off the H sound turns 'habit' into ''abit', heard as 'a bit', which is 'not a lot'.
explanation.definitionFit: Omitting the H at the start of words, a Cockney speech trait, makes 'habit' sound like 'a bit'.

clue.text: Commercial breaks are initially mesmerising client

indicators.note: breaks means these letters are smashed and reassembled

parts.note: the words are and client are taken as written, with only the first letter of mesmerising, signalled by initially, between them

explanation.surface: Adverts interrupt and hypnotise a viewer or customer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commercial breaks' looks like TV ads; 'breaks' is the anagram signal, and 'initially' keeps only the M of 'mesmerising' for the pool ARE + M + CLIENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to trade and merchants, a synonym for commercial.

clue.text: Appliance as it should be without French president

parts.note: a fridge should be cool

indicators.note: without means the abbreviation for French is taken out

parts.note: a fridge is a kitchen appliance

explanation.surface: A kitchen appliance that works well, lacking a French leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French president' suggests Macron or similar; 'president' alone is the definition, 30th of the US.
explanation.definitionFit: Calvin Coolidge was the 30th president of the United States, from 1923 to 1929.

clue.text: Catch on in the end

indicators.note: in means the small word is placed within the vulgar term for the rear

parts.note: a vulgar word for the backside, one's rear end

explanation.surface: Someone finally understands something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch on' wants to be 'understand'; 'Catch' is the definition and ON goes in a crude word for the behind.
explanation.definitionFit: To detain someone in conversation against their will, to accost or catch them.

clue.text: Notice in defect, nasty piece of work

indicators.note: in means the word for notice sits inside the word for defect

parts.note: a blot is a flaw or blemish
an ad is a notice or advertisement

explanation.surface: A notice reveals a fault, and someone unpleasant is responsible.
explanation.definitionFit: An unpleasant, untrustworthy person, a rotter or villain.

clue.text: So, best ten bananas fed to gorilla, I say!

indicators.note: fed to means the scrambled letters go inside the word for gorilla

parts.note: a heavy is a thug or minder, also known as a gorilla

indicators.note: bananas means crazy, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A zookeeper's report: the best bananas were fed to the ape, and wow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bananas' looks like the food; it is the anagram signal on SO BEST TEN. A 'gorilla' is slang for a thug, a heavy.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned American exclamation of surprise, like 'goodness me'.

clue.text: Nipper in loft, back shortly

parts.note: to loft a ball is to lob it high

indicators.note: shortly means the word for back loses its last letter

parts.note: the stern is the back of a ship

explanation.surface: A child up in the attic will be back soon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nipper' looks like a child; it is a creature with claws.
explanation.definitionFit: A crustacean with pincers that nip, so jokingly a nipper.

clue.text: See 13
South American relations in historical county

parts.note: US means American
sexual relations, sex

explanation.surface: South Americans have family ties in an old English shire.
explanation.walkthrough: SUSSEX is a historical county in south-east England, now split into East and West Sussex.
explanation.definitionFit: The old county of the South Saxons, now divided into two administrative counties.

clue.text: Hang out first of washing in valley

indicators.note: in means the single letter goes within the word for valley

parts.note: a dell is a small wooded valley

indicators.note: first of takes the opening letter of washing

explanation.surface: Instructions to peg out laundry down in a valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hang out' suggests laundry; it means to live or linger.
explanation.definitionFit: To reside or stay in a place, as when one hangs out somewhere.

clue.text: A strike on head of robin in death — accursed bird?

indicators.note: in means the strike and robin's initial sit within the word for death

parts.note: a death is a loss
to bat is to strike

indicators.note: head of takes the first letter of robin

explanation.surface: A bird is struck and dies, a cursed killing.
explanation.walkthrough: In Coleridge's 'Rime of the Ancient Mariner', shooting this bird brings a curse.
explanation.definitionFit: Literary allusion: the mariner kills the seabird and is cursed, so it is the bird linked to a curse.

clue.text: Cord matching rope, ultimately

parts.note: twin means matching, as in twin beds

indicators.note: ultimately takes the final letter of rope

explanation.surface: A string that matches the rope, in the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Strong string or thin cord made of twisted strands.

clue.text: Lord's period noble after abdication of king — outstanding!

parts.note: Lord's is the London cricket ground, and an over is a period of six balls in cricket

indicators.note: after abdication of means the king letter has left the word for noble

parts.note: a duke is a noble
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A lord's time of nobility after a king steps down, cheered as brilliant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outstanding!' looks like praise; it means still unpaid. LORD'S is a London cricket ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Unpaid or late, still outstanding in the sense of not yet settled.

clue.text: Old vessel shipshape, on boarding, expedition's beginning

indicators.note: boarding means getting on, so the small word goes inside the word for shipshape

parts.note: trim means neat and shipshape
re means on or about

indicators.note: beginning takes the first letter of expedition

explanation.surface: A tidy ship, crew boarding, at the start of a voyage.
explanation.definitionFit: An ancient galley with three banks of oars, used by Greeks and Romans.

clue.text: Welshman with desire to put in effort, saw work?

indicators.note: to put in means these pieces go inside the word for effort

parts.note: a try is an effort or attempt
Rees is a common Welsh name
an urge is a desire

explanation.surface: A Welshman wants to make an effort at some saw-related task.
explanation.walkthrough: 'saw work' could be carpentry; it is cutting branches.
explanation.definitionFit: Arboriculture: pruning and felling trees, work done with a saw.
